This vignette introduces the Human Tumor Atlas Network (HTAN) and the
*HTAN* package. It covers what the program is, how its data are organised and
where they are stored, and what the package can and cannot do. It ends with a
short tour of the package. Three companion vignettes go further:

- [The HTAN data model, identifiers and lineage](data-model.html) explains
  the identifiers, the metadata tables, and how a processed file is traced
  back to a biospecimen and a participant.
- [Exploring the HTAN Phase 1 atlas](atlas-overview.html) is a descriptive
  tour of the whole Phase 1 release: centers, organs, assays, data levels
  and clinical variables.
- [From query to analysis](analysis-workflow.html) works through one
  dataset, from a metadata query to a spatial transcriptomics analysis in
  Bioconductor.

The output in these vignettes was computed ahead of time from the real HTAN
Release 7 metadata (see [How these vignettes are built](#how-these-vignettes-are-built)).

# Getting started

Install the package from GitHub with BiocManager:


``` r
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("seandavi/HTAN")
```

Load it, together with dplyr, which is the query language for everything
that follows:


``` r
library(HTAN)
library(dplyr)
```

Open a connection to the Release 7 metadata snapshot. The first call
downloads about 20 MB of parquet files from Hugging Face, checks each one
against its sha256 checksum and caches it; later calls read from the cache.
No account is needed.


``` r
con <- htan_con("r7")
```

Find files. `htan_files()` returns one row per HTAN data file, as a lazy
table that runs in DuckDB until you call `collect()`:


``` r
htan_files(assay == "ScRNA-seq", level == 4, con = con) |>
    count(HTAN_Center, extension) |>
    arrange(desc(n)) |>
    collect()
#> # A tibble: 12 × 3
#>    HTAN_Center     extension     n
#>    <chr>           <chr>     <dbl>
#>  1 HTAN WUSTL      .rds        237
#>  2 HTAN CHOP       .rds        197
#>  3 HTAN MSK        .csv        191
#>  4 HTAN MSK        .txt         76
#>  5 HTAN DFCI       .h5ad        48
#>  6 HTAN HTAPP      .tsv         47
#>  7 HTAN BU         .csv         32
#>  8 HTAN MSK        .h5ad        15
#>  9 HTAN CHOP       .tsv          6
#> 10 HTAN Vanderbilt .h5ad         6
#> 11 HTAN CHOP       .h5ad         1
#> 12 HTAN Duke       .rds          1
```

Trace a processed file back to the raw files and biospecimen it came from:


``` r
htan_files(assay == "ScRNA-seq", level == 4, participants = "HTA12_251",
    con = con) |>
    head(1) |>
    htan_lineage(con = con) |>
    select(related_file_id, depth, Component, HTAN_Assayed_Biospecimen_ID) |>
    arrange(depth) |>
    collect()
#> # A tibble: 13 × 4
#>    related_file_id depth Component        HTAN_Assayed_Biospecimen_ID
#>    <chr>           <int> <chr>            <chr>                      
#>  1 HTA12_251_1000     -3 ScRNA-seqLevel1  HTA12_251_3                
#>  2 HTA12_251_1014     -3 ScATAC-seqLevel1 HTA12_251_3                
#>  3 HTA12_251_1002     -3 ScRNA-seqLevel1  HTA12_251_3                
#>  4 HTA12_251_1003     -3 ScRNA-seqLevel1  HTA12_251_3                
#>  5 HTA12_251_1013     -3 ScATAC-seqLevel1 HTA12_251_3                
#>  6 HTA12_251_1015     -3 ScATAC-seqLevel1 HTA12_251_3                
#>  7 HTA12_251_1001     -3 ScRNA-seqLevel1  HTA12_251_3                
#>  8 HTA12_251_2000     -2 ScRNA-seqLevel2  HTA12_251_3                
#>  9 HTA12_251_2002     -2 ScATAC-seqLevel2 HTA12_251_3                
#> 10 HTA12_251_3001     -1 ScATAC-seqLevel3 HTA12_251_3                
#> 11 HTA12_251_3002     -1 ScATAC-seqLevel3 HTA12_251_3                
#> 12 HTA12_251_3003     -1 ScATAC-seqLevel3 HTA12_251_3                
#> 13 HTA12_251_4000      0 ScRNA-seqLevel4  HTA12_251_3
```

Download an open file. Level 2 images in the CRDC General Commons need no
account; processed Level 3 and 4 files are on Synapse and need a free
personal access token (see [Downloading files](#downloading-files)). Then
read the file with `read_htan()`, which returns a Bioconductor object where
it can.

That is the whole workflow: query, trace, download, read. The rest of this
vignette explains what you are querying.

# What HTAN is

The Human Tumor Atlas Network is a National Cancer Institute (NCI) Cancer
Moonshot initiative, launched in September 2018, that builds
three-dimensional atlases of the cellular, morphological and molecular
features of human cancers ([HTAN overview](https://humantumoratlas.org/overview)).
The founding paper (Rozenblatt-Rosen et al., *Cell* 2020;
[doi:10.1016/j.cell.2020.03.053](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2020.03.053),
PMID 32302568) frames the program around *transitions*: the points at which
a tumour's behaviour changes, such as

- the progression of a precancerous lesion to invasive cancer,
- local expansion and metastasis, and
- the response of a tumour to therapy and the emergence of resistance.

Bulk sequencing of a single tumour sample averages over every cell in it and
records one moment in time. HTAN's premise is that these transitions are
driven by the interactions between tumour cells, immune cells, stroma and
vasculature, and that seeing them needs measurements at single-cell
resolution, in spatial context, and across time. HTAN centers therefore
combine single-cell and single-nucleus sequencing, spatial transcriptomics,
multiplexed tissue imaging, and conventional bulk sequencing and pathology,
on biospecimens with detailed clinical annotation. Many participants
contribute several biospecimens: serial sections of one block, several
regions of a resection, or samples taken before and after treatment.

## Phase 1

Phase 1 had ten Research Centers, each building an atlas of one or more
cancer types, and two NCI pilot projects, the Human Tumor Atlas Pilot
Project (HTAPP) and the Pre-Cancer Atlas Pilot Project (PCAPP). A single
Data Coordinating Center (DCC) set the data standards, ran ingestion and
validation, and built the portal and the other routes to the data ([HTAN overview](https://humantumoratlas.org/overview);
de Bruijn et al., *Nature Methods* 2025,
[doi:10.1038/s41592-025-02643-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-025-02643-0)).
Four Trans-Network Projects (TNPs) compared technologies across centers. The
HTAN manual lists every Phase 1 center with its identifier prefix
([HTAN centers](https://docs.humantumoratlas.org/overview/centers/)):

| Prefix | Center | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| HTA1 | Human Tumor Atlas Pilot Project (HTAPP) | Pilot project |
| HTA2 | Pre-Cancer Atlas Pilot Project (PCAPP) | Pilot project |
| HTA3 | Boston University | Lung |
| HTA4 | Children's Hospital of Philadelphia | Pediatric |
| HTA5 | Dana-Farber Cancer Institute | Multiple cancer types |
| HTA6 | Duke University | Breast |
| HTA7 | Harvard Medical School | Melanoma, colorectal cancer, clonal hematopoiesis |
| HTA8 | Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center | Multiple cancer types |
| HTA9 | Oregon Health & Science University | Breast |
| HTA10 | Stanford University | Familial adenomatous polyposis |
| HTA11 | Vanderbilt University | Colorectal |
| HTA12 | Washington University in St. Louis | Multiple cancer types |
| HTA13 | TNP: SARDANA | Technology comparison |
| HTA14 | TNP: Tissue MicroArray (TMA) | Technology comparison |
| HTA15 | TNP: SRRS | Technology comparison |
| HTA16 | TNP: CASI | Technology comparison |

Phase 1 data were released in seven numbered releases between May 2021 and
November 2025 ([data release history](https://data.humantumoratlas.org/data-updates)).
Release 7, published on 2025-11-26, is the last Phase 1 release and the one
this package targets. The Phase 1 data model is archived
([ncihtan/data-models](https://github.com/ncihtan/data-models)), so the
release is effectively frozen. The DCC's 2025 paper counts 8,425
biospecimens from 2,042 participants profiled with more than 20 assays; it
was written before Release 7, and the [atlas overview](atlas-overview.html)
recounts everything from the Release 7 tables themselves.

## Phase 2

Phase 2 funds ten new atlases, five of pre-cancer and five of cancer, with
identifier prefixes HTA200 to HTA209. Its first data release, on
2026-08-03, was 50 files from 11 participants of the prostate atlas
([data release history](https://data.humantumoratlas.org/data-updates)).
Phase 2 uses a new data model, aligned with the NCI Cancer Research Data
Commons, that changes file formats, valid values and attributes, and marks
biospecimen and data file identifiers with `B` and `D`
([HTAN data model overview](https://docs.humantumoratlas.org/data_model/overview/),
[identifiers](https://docs.humantumoratlas.org/data_model/identifiers/)).
That model is still changing, and the ISB-CGC BigQuery tables for Phase 2
did not exist when this package was written. **This package covers Phase 1
only.** Phase 2 will be added once its tables settle.

# How HTAN data are organised

## Participants, biospecimens and files

Every HTAN record hangs from a three-level hierarchy:

1. A **participant** is a research participant (a patient or donor), with
   clinical data: demographics, diagnosis, therapy, follow-up and more.
2. A **biospecimen** is something taken from a participant (a biopsy, a
   resection, a blood draw) or derived from another biospecimen (a block,
   a section, a dissociated cell suspension, an extracted analyte).
3. A **data file** is the output of an assay run on a biospecimen, or a
   file computed from other files.

Each level has an HTAN identifier that starts with the center prefix:
`HTA11_7862` is a participant at Vanderbilt, `HTA11_7862_2000001011` is one
of that participant's biospecimens, and `HTA11_7862_200000101134111` is a
data file. The [data model vignette](data-model.html) covers the
identifier grammar and its exceptions in detail.

## Data levels

Every assay's files are grouped into *levels*, from raw instrument output to
analysis-ready summaries. The HTAN manual defines them per assay
([file standards](https://docs.humantumoratlas.org/data_model/file_standards/),
[metadata standards](https://docs.humantumoratlas.org/data_model/metadata_standards/)).
In outline:

| Level | Sequencing (scRNA-seq, bulk, scATAC-seq) | Multiplexed imaging (CyCIF, CODEX, MIBI, H&E, ...) | 10x Visium |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Raw reads: FASTQ, unaligned BAM | Raw tiles before stitching and registration (rarely submitted) | FASTQ |
| 2 | Aligned reads: BAM | One assembled image, preferably a tiled, pyramidal OME-TIFF | Aligned BAM |
| 3 | Derived molecular data: gene-by-cell count matrices, VCFs | Segmentation masks, validated channel metadata, QC'd image | Space Ranger output: counts, spot positions, tissue image |
| 4 | Sample-level summaries: annotated objects, embeddings, clusters | A cell-by-feature table (marker intensities, centroids, morphology) | Processed objects: clusters, embeddings, `.h5ad` or `.rds` |

Other assays follow the same idea. RPPA has no Level 1; mass spectrometry
runs from raw spectra (Level 1) to protein abundance (Level 4); and some
newer assays, such as 10x Xenium, are submitted as a single experiment
bundle instead of separate levels. Auxiliary files (for example Visium
alignment images and QC reports) and "Other Assay" files have no level.

In practice most users start at Level 3 or 4: a count matrix or an
annotated single-cell object, or a cell-by-marker table for imaging. Those
are the files this package reads.

## Access tiers

HTAN data are released in two tiers
([data access](https://docs.humantumoratlas.org/data_access/introduction/)):

- **Open access**: all metadata (clinical, biospecimen and file-level),
  multiplexed and H&E images, and processed (Level 3 and 4) genomic data.
- **Controlled access**: unprocessed genomic data (Level 1 and 2 sequencing:
  FASTQ and BAM files), which could identify a participant. Access is
  through dbGaP study
  [phs002371](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/projects/gap/cgi-bin/study.cgi?study_id=phs002371).

The package records the tier of each file in the `access` column of
`htan_files()`, with open files split by where they can be fetched from.

## Where the data live, and why

HTAN data are spread across several NCI and partner systems, each chosen for
one job:

| System | Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [Synapse](https://www.synapse.org) (Sage Bionetworks) | Open Level 3 and 4 files, auxiliary files, submitted metadata | Free account and personal access token |
| [CRDC General Commons](https://datacommons.cancer.gov/repository/general-commons) | Controlled Level 1/2 sequencing; open Level 2 images | dbGaP authorisation for controlled data; open images anonymously through GA4GH DRS |
| [Imaging Data Commons](https://portal.imaging.datacommons.cancer.gov/) (IDC) | DICOM conversions of some HTAN slide images | Anonymous |
| ISB-CGC BigQuery (`isb-cgc-bq.HTAN`, `isb-cgc-bq.HTAN_versioned`) | All open metadata tables, plus some processed expression and cell tables | Google Cloud account and a billing project |
| [HTAN Data Portal](https://humantumoratlas.org/explore) | Search, summaries and manifests for every tier | Browser |

Synapse is the DCC's ingestion platform: centers upload files and
metadata there, and the DCC validates and releases them. The CRDC General
Commons is NCI's long-term repository, and the only one of these systems
that can hold dbGaP-controlled data. It also serves the open images,
because image files are large and the CRDC is built for cloud-scale storage.
IDC converts a subset of the slides to DICOM so they can be viewed in a
browser alongside other NCI imaging collections. ISB-CGC loads every
release's metadata into BigQuery for SQL analysis in Google Cloud
([HTAN BigQuery](https://docs.humantumoratlas.org/data_access/biq_query/),
[ISB-CGC HTAN notebooks](https://isb-cancer-genomics-cloud.readthedocs.io/en/latest/sections/HTANNotebooks.html)).

For an R user, the consequence is that finding a file and fetching it are
separate problems. The metadata tell you which files exist and how they
relate; the file itself is on Synapse or the CRDC, behind different
authentication.

# What this package does, and what it doesn't

*HTAN* is a client for the **open-access data of HTAN Phase 1**. It does
five things:

1. **Query metadata locally.** `htan_con()` opens a DuckDB connection over
   a parquet snapshot of the ISB-CGC Release 7 metadata tables;
   `htan_tables()`, `htan_tbl()` and `htan_columns()` list, open and
   describe them; `htan_files()` gives one row per file with its assay,
   level, participants, biospecimens and access tier. Queries are dplyr
   code translated to SQL by dbplyr, so they run in DuckDB and only the
   result is pulled into R.
2. **Trace lineage.** `htan_lineage()` walks the `id_provenance` table from
   a file to its ancestors (down to Level 1 and the biospecimen) or its
   descendants.
3. **Download open files.** `htan_download()` fetches open Level 2 images
   anonymously from the CRDC General Commons, and Level 3/4 files from
   Synapse with a personal access token. It checks each file's md5 and
   guards against accidentally large downloads.
4. **Read files into Bioconductor classes.** `read_htan()` turns `.h5ad`,
   `.rds` (including Seurat objects), 10x `.h5`, Space Ranger output and
   imaging cell tables into `SingleCellExperiment` or `SpatialExperiment`
   objects.
5. **Assemble a `MultiAssayExperiment`.** `htan_experiment()` combines
   objects from several files, linking every cell or spot to its
   participant and attaching clinical data.

It does **not**:

- download controlled-access data (it stops with a pointer to dbGaP and the
  CRDC tools);
- cover HTAN Phase 2;
- query the large processed tables in BigQuery (single-cell expression and
  imaging cell tables, about 2.4 TB), or BigQuery at all;
- query IDC, CELLxGENE or the HTAN portal's database;
- analyse images (images are returned as paths, for RBioFormats or
  cytomapper).

Level 4 files are heterogeneous: each center chose its own object classes,
assay names and annotations. `read_htan()` is best effort, and you should
check what it returns.

# The metadata snapshot

## What it is

ISB-CGC publishes HTAN's metadata in two BigQuery datasets: `HTAN`, whose
`_current` tables always point at the newest release, and
`HTAN_versioned`, which keeps every release's tables under names such as
`clinical_tier1_demographics_r7`. The snapshot is an export of the 78 tables
that make up Release 7, each pinned to its versioned copy, written as zstd
parquet with a manifest of checksums. It is published as the Hugging Face
dataset [`seandavis/htan`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/seandavis/htan),
one git tag per release, so `htan_con("r7")` always reads the same bytes.


``` r
info <- htan_snapshot_info(con)
info[c("release", "phase", "source", "n_tables", "total_rows", "build_date")]
#> $release
#> [1] "r7"
#> 
#> $phase
#> [1] "1"
#> 
#> $source
#> [1] "isb-cgc-bq.HTAN_versioned"
#> 
#> $n_tables
#> [1] "78"
#> 
#> $total_rows
#> [1] "821773"
#> 
#> $build_date
#> [1] "2026-10-14T11:53:18Z"
```

The tables fall into two groups: clinical and biospecimen tables, and
metadata tables (one or more per assay and level, plus `id_provenance`,
`gc_drs_map` and the data-model `schema`):


``` r
htan_tables(con) |>
    count(category)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   category                      n
#>   <chr>                     <int>
#> 1 clinical_biospecimen_data    16
#> 2 metadata                     62
```

A few tables were not refreshed in Release 7, so the snapshot takes them
from the last release that had them:


``` r
htan_tables(con) |>
    filter(source_version != "r7") |>
    select(name, source_version, rows)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   name                                        source_version  rows
#>   <chr>                                       <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 imaging_level1_metadata                     r6_v2             16
#> 2 lipidomics_metadata                         r2_v2             84
#> 3 metabolomics_metadata                       r2_v2            176
#> 4 proteomics_metadata                         r2               392
#> 5 publication_manifest_metadata               r5                 1
#> 6 tissueOrOrganOfOrigin_to_wholeOrgan_mapping r4               332
```

## How it relates to the authoritative sources

The snapshot is a copy of a copy. The DCC's records in Synapse are the
source of truth; ISB-CGC derives its BigQuery tables from them at each
release; the snapshot is an export of those tables at one release. That has
three consequences:

- **It can lag or differ.** If the HTAN portal and the snapshot disagree,
  the portal is right. Fixes made by the DCC after Release 7 reach the
  snapshot only if ISB-CGC republishes the r7 tables and the snapshot is
  rebuilt.
- **It is unofficial.** The DCC does not host or endorse it. It
  redistributes open-access metadata; HTAN's terms of use still apply, and
  work that uses the data should cite HTAN's publications, as the
  [HTAN manual](https://docs.humantumoratlas.org/data_access/citing_htan/)
  asks.
- **It holds metadata only.** File contents stay on Synapse and the CRDC.

The trade is convenience: the snapshot needs no Google account or billing
project, works offline once cached, and answers most questions in
milliseconds. You can also browse it without R: the Hugging Face page has a
data viewer and a SQL console, and DuckDB reads the files directly as
`hf://datasets/seandavis/htan@r7/<table>.parquet`.

To use a mirror or a local build, set `options(HTAN.base_url = ...)`. The
package also ships a tiny fixture of the snapshot (all 78 tables cut down to
six participants), which its examples and tests use:


``` r
fixture <- system.file("extdata", "snapshot", package = "HTAN")
con_small <- htan_con("r7", base_url = fixture)
```

# A quick tour

## Tables and columns

`htan_tbl()` opens any table lazily. Here are the participants'
demographics, summarised in DuckDB:


``` r
htan_tbl("clinical_tier1_demographics", con) |>
    count(Gender, sort = TRUE) |>
    collect()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   Gender           n
#>   <chr>        <dbl>
#> 1 Female        1454
#> 2 Male           547
#> 3 female         418
#> 4 Not Reported   193
#> 5 male           183
#> 6 unknown         10
```

The same value is spelled several ways: centers submitted their own
metadata, and the DCC's validation did not normalise case. Clean values
before you count or join on them:


``` r
htan_tbl("clinical_tier1_demographics", con) |>
    mutate(Gender = tolower(Gender)) |>
    count(Gender, sort = TRUE) |>
    collect()
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   Gender           n
#>   <chr>        <dbl>
#> 1 female        1872
#> 2 male           730
#> 3 not reported   193
#> 4 unknown         10
```

`htan_columns()` returns the column descriptions recorded in the BigQuery
schema, which is the quickest way to learn what a field means:


``` r
htan_columns("id_provenance", con) |>
    select(column, description)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 2
#>    column                          description                                  
#>    <chr>                           <chr>                                        
#>  1 HTAN_Data_File_ID               Self-identifier for this data file - HTAN ID…
#>  2 Filename                        Name of a file                               
#>  3 entityId                        Synapse ID of entity                         
#>  4 Component                       Category of metadata (e.g. Diagnosis, Biospe…
#>  5 Data_Release                    Inclusion in HTAN Data Release e.g. Release …
#>  6 GC_Release                      Released to CRDC’s General Commons (GC) as p…
#>  7 HTAN_Center                     Name of HTAN Center e.g. HTAN HTAPP          
#>  8 HTAN_Assayed_Biospecimen_ID     HTAN ID of the biospecimen directly assayed …
#>  9 HTAN_Parent_Data_File_ID        HTAN Data File Identifier indicating the fil…
#> 10 HTAN_Originating_Biospecimen_ID HTAN ID of the biopsied or resected biospeci…
#> 11 HTAN_Participant_ID             HTAN ID associated with a patient based on H…
#> 12 Biospecimen_Path                Full Biospecimen ancestry path from HTAN_Ass…
```

## Files

`htan_files()` combines every file-level table in the snapshot. Its columns
include the `Component` (the assay and level, as HTAN names it), `assay` and
`level` split out of it, the file `extension`, size and md5, the Synapse
`entityId`, the General Commons `drs_uri`, the participants and
biospecimens from `id_provenance`, and the `access` tier:


``` r
files <- htan_files(con = con)
files |>
    count(access) |>
    arrange(desc(n)) |>
    collect()
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   access            n
#>   <chr>         <dbl>
#> 1 open-synapse 154520
#> 2 controlled    42897
#> 3 open-gc       24271
```

There are 221,688 files in Release 7. The tiers are:

- `open-gc`: open Level 2 images in the General Commons, downloadable
  anonymously;
- `open-synapse`: open files on Synapse (Level 3/4, auxiliary and other
  files, and the images that were never copied to the General Commons),
  downloadable with a token;
- `controlled`: Level 1/2 sequencing under dbGaP, which the package will
  not download.

Filters go straight into `htan_files()`. For example, every open
single-cell Level 4 file in AnnData format:


``` r
htan_files(assay == "ScRNA-seq", level == 4, extension == ".h5ad",
    con = con) |>
    select(HTAN_Data_File_ID, HTAN_Center, File_Size, n_participants) |>
    arrange(File_Size) |>
    collect()
#> # A tibble: 70 × 4
#>    HTAN_Data_File_ID HTAN_Center File_Size n_participants
#>    <chr>             <chr>           <dbl>          <dbl>
#>  1 HTA5_0000_1003255 HTAN DFCI    11599590              4
#>  2 HTA5_0000_1003254 HTAN DFCI    12396714              4
#>  3 HTA5_0000_1003271 HTAN DFCI    24735020              4
#>  4 HTA5_0000_1003281 HTAN DFCI    30191344              4
#>  5 HTA5_0000_1003295 HTAN DFCI    32403150              4
#>  6 HTA5_0000_1003261 HTAN DFCI    34842022              4
#>  7 HTA5_0000_1003274 HTAN DFCI    37313138              4
#>  8 HTA5_0000_1003284 HTAN DFCI    38056449              4
#>  9 HTA5_0000_1003243 HTAN DFCI    39081430              4
#> 10 HTA5_0000_1003257 HTAN DFCI    40003858              4
#> # ℹ 60 more rows
```

Some files, such as merged single-cell objects, come from several
participants; their `HTAN_Participant_ID` is a comma-separated list. To find
every file that involves a participant, use the `participants` argument,
which handles that case, rather than `==`:


``` r
htan_files(participants = "HTA11_7862", con = con) |>
    count(Component, access) |>
    arrange(Component) |>
    collect()
#> # A tibble: 13 × 3
#>    Component                                      access           n
#>    <chr>                                          <chr>        <dbl>
#>  1 10xVisiumSpatialTranscriptomics-AuxiliaryFiles open-synapse     1
#>  2 10xVisiumSpatialTranscriptomics-RNA-seqLevel1  controlled       2
#>  3 10xVisiumSpatialTranscriptomics-RNA-seqLevel2  controlled       1
#>  4 10xVisiumSpatialTranscriptomics-RNA-seqLevel3  open-synapse     4
#>  5 10xVisiumSpatialTranscriptomics-RNA-seqLevel4  open-synapse     1
#>  6 BulkWESLevel1                                  controlled       4
#>  7 BulkWESLevel2                                  controlled       2
#>  8 BulkWESLevel3                                  open-synapse     1
#>  9 ImagingLevel2                                  open-synapse     3
#> 10 ScRNA-seqLevel1                                controlled       6
#> 11 ScRNA-seqLevel2                                controlled       3
#> 12 ScRNA-seqLevel3                                open-synapse     3
#> 13 ScRNA-seqLevel4                                open-synapse     4
```

That one participant, from the Vanderbilt colorectal atlas, has Visium
spatial transcriptomics, single-cell RNA-seq, whole-exome sequencing and
imaging. The [analysis vignette](analysis-workflow.html) uses their Visium
data.

## Lineage

`htan_lineage()` follows `HTAN_Parent_Data_File_ID` links in
`id_provenance`. Depth 0 is the query file; negative depths are its
ancestors:


``` r
htan_lineage("HTA11_7862_200000101134111", con = con) |>
    select(related_file_id, depth, Filename) |>
    arrange(depth, related_file_id) |>
    collect() |>
    mutate(Filename = basename(Filename))
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>   related_file_id            depth Filename                            
#>   <chr>                      <int> <chr>                               
#> 1 HTA11_7862_200000101131111    -3 8270-AS-0001_S1_L005_R1_001.fastq.gz
#> 2 HTA11_7862_200000101131121    -3 8270-AS-0001_S1_L005_R2_001.fastq.gz
#> 3 HTA11_7862_200000101132111    -2 8270_AS_1_possorted_genome_bam.bam  
#> 4 HTA11_7862_200000101133111    -1 8270_AS_1_barcodes.tsv.gz           
#> 5 HTA11_7862_200000101133121    -1 8270_AS_1_features.tsv.gz           
#> 6 HTA11_7862_200000101133131    -1 8270_AS_1_matrix.mtx.gz             
#> 7 HTA11_7862_200000101133141    -1 8270_AS_1_tissue_positions_list.csv 
#> 8 HTA11_7862_200000101134111     0 8270_AS_1_unfiltered.h5ad
```

The Level 4 Visium object was computed from four Level 3 Space Ranger
files, which came from a Level 2 alignment, which came from two Level 1
FASTQ files. The [data model vignette](data-model.html) explains how these
links are recorded and where they get complicated.

## Downloading files

`htan_download()` routes each file by its `access` tier, checks its md5,
and returns a table of local paths. An open image in the General Commons
needs no account. This one is a 250 KB imaging mass cytometry image:


``` r
tiff <- htan_files(
    drs_uri == "dg.4DFC/6231a7d4-7e68-11ee-b51d-e7db3b9207b8", con = con)
tiff |>
    select(HTAN_Data_File_ID, Component, File_Size, access) |>
    collect()
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   HTAN_Data_File_ID Component     File_Size access 
#>   <chr>             <chr>             <dbl> <chr>  
#> 1 HTA12_15_1105     ImagingLevel2    254833 open-gc
dl <- htan_download(tiff, dest = tempfile("htan-"), con = con)
dl$status
#> [1] "downloaded"
read_htan(dl) |> basename()
#> [1] "HTAN_HT166P1_S1H5_L4_ROI_001.ome.tiff"
```

`read_htan()` returns image paths unchanged; RBioFormats or cytomapper can
read them.

Processed files are on Synapse. To fetch them:

1. create a free account at <https://www.synapse.org>;
2. make a personal access token (Account Settings, then Personal Access
   Tokens) with download permission;
3. put it in the `SYNAPSE_AUTH_TOKEN` environment variable, for example in
   `~/.Renviron`, and restart R.


``` r
visium <- htan_files(HTAN_Data_File_ID == "HTA11_7862_200000101134111",
    con = con)
dl <- htan_download(visium, dest = "htan-data", con = con)
spe <- read_htan(dl)
```

Some HTAN files are tens of gigabytes. `htan_download()` refuses to start if
the files total more than `max_bytes` (20 GB by default), and skips files
already present with the right md5. Controlled files are refused with a
classed error:


``` r
fastq <- htan_files(access == "controlled", con = con) |>
    arrange(HTAN_Data_File_ID) |>
    head(1)
tryCatch(
    htan_download(fastq, dest = tempfile(), con = con),
    htan_error_controlled = function(e) cat(conditionMessage(e))
)
#> Controlled-access files cannot be downloaded by HTAN.
#> ✖ HTA10_0000_42410718832338308254033538547980
#> ℹ Level 1/2 sequencing is under dbGaP phs002371; request access, then use the CRDC gen3-client.
#> ℹ Drop them with `filter(access != "controlled")`.
```

## Reading and assembling

`read_htan()` dispatches on the file extension:

| File | Returns |
|---|---|
| `.h5ad` | `SingleCellExperiment` (via anndataR), or `SpatialExperiment` when there is a spatial embedding |
| `.rds`, `.RData` | the object; Seurat objects become `SingleCellExperiment` |
| 10x `.h5` | `SingleCellExperiment` (via TENxIO) |
| Space Ranger `outs/` directory | `SpatialExperiment` (via VisiumIO) |
| Imaging Level 4 `.csv` cell table | `SpatialExperiment`, cells as columns |
| `.tif`, `.ome.tiff`, `.svs` | the path |

`htan_experiment()` then builds a `MultiAssayExperiment` from a named list
of objects, using the file IDs to find each object's participant and
attaching that participant's demographics and diagnosis as `colData`. The
[analysis vignette](analysis-workflow.html) does this with real data.

# How these vignettes are built

Bioconductor builds packages on machines without credentials and without
network access, but these vignettes read the snapshot from Hugging Face,
and one downloads from Synapse. So each vignette is written as a
`.qmd.orig` source in the package repository and run ahead of time by
`dev/precompute-vignettes.R` (`just precompute-vignettes`), which writes
the `.qmd` you are reading, with its output and figures. Building the
package only renders that markdown. The numbers in these vignettes are
therefore the numbers at the time they were last precomputed; with a
release pinned to `r7`, they should not change.
